quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

The Great Register gives the clearest picture — his exact address (5 Cook Street, Ward 9), the court that naturalized him, and that he was 21 years old. Both of these records have been tentatively matched to Hermann Gaetjen in the family tree at the lowest level of confidence, because two other men named Hermann Gaetjen are known to have lived in California at overlapping times — until a record also names his wife Amelia or one of his children, the system cannot rule them out with full confidence, and so no details from either record have yet been added to his profile in the tree.

Finding a marriage record for Hermann and Amelia, or any record naming him alongside his children, is the step that would confirm the match and allow the immigration and registration details to be formally attached to his tree entry.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire destroyed City Hall and the Hall of Records. Pre-1906 county-level civil birth, marriage, and death certificates were largely destroyed. Substitute sources (church records, funeral home records, Great Registers, newspapers) are essential for the entire 1850-1905 period.

San Francisco passenger arrival lists for approximately 1865-1892 are not digitized or name-indexed online. NARA microfilm reels (M261 and predecessor series) must be consulted in person at the National Archives at San Francisco (San Bruno, CA) or by mail request.

The Great Register (voter register) states each registrant's nativity, naturalization court, and naturalization date — the highest-priority substitute source when passenger lists and pre-1906 vital records are unavailable. FamilySearch collection 1935764 (3.3 million records, indexed) and Ancestry Voter Registers 1866-1898 (indexed + images).

Naturalization before 1880 was in the state district court (or county court 1862-1880); after 1880 in the superior court. San Francisco is also a federal district court seat, so many immigrants naturalized under the Northern District Court — covered by FamilySearch collection 1849982.

Declarations of intention (first papers) from the US Northern District Court 1846-1903 are at the National Archives, San Bruno (also FamilySearch Library films 977767-70). These may predate final citizenship by years and often name German hometown.
The 1900 census is the most direct online source for an immigrant's year of arrival — it asks for year of immigration and years in the US. The 1880 census records only birthplace.

North German surname Gaetjen (Low German patronymic, Oldenburg/Hannover/East Friesland region) — search Hamburg departure lists (Ancestry, partially indexed 1877-1914) as departure records often name the emigrant's home village. North Germans disproportionately used Hamburg over Bremen.

Bremen departure lists are largely destroyed; only 1907-1908 and 1913-1914 card index and a partial 1920-1939 reconstruction survive. Baltimore arrival lists partially compensate for Bremen-departing immigrants.

San Francisco funeral home records (FamilySearch collection 1385518, 162,363 records, indexed + images) survived 1906 and often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — more detailed than civil death certificates.

The 1904 death certificate volumes (nine digitized volumes from FamilySearch volume search) are 0% name-indexed but full-text searchable — use FamilySearch full-text search to locate Gaetjen without browsing image by image.
Many original San Francisco cemeteries were relocated to Colma (San Mateo County) in the early 20th century — search San Mateo County records for burial information.
Search name variants: Gaetjen, Gaetgen, Gätjen, Gärtjen, and anglicized or misspelled forms with plain a or e instead of ae/ä.

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → Patrick Flynn / I1)

The person-evidence agent completed a full audit of pe_005. Here is its assessment:

---

### What pe_005 links
**a_013** is the parentage relationship assertion ("Father: Thomas Flynn") from the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (src_004). The informant is James Brown, son-in-law — a secondary informant, not present at the events recorded.

---

### Verdict: `confident` is **not justified**

Three substantive problems undermine the calibration:

---

#### Issue 1 — No `same_person` score obtained
The rule is explicit: without a similarity score of **≥ 0.75**, a single-source qualitative link is capped at **`probable`**, never `confident`. `pe_005` has `match_score: null` and the rationale does not explain why the score was skipped or whether the persona was unreachable.

#### Issue 2 — Birthplace conflict unacknowledged
`a_012` (from the same record, same persona) notes: *"death cert says Pennsylvania, but census records say Ireland."* This is a core identifier conflict. The rules require that every `pe_` entry for this persona either flag the conflict in `core_identifier_conflict` or explicitly clear it in the rationale. Neither happened. A plausible clearing explanation exists — the son-in-law informant was secondary and not present at Patrick's birth, so substituting Pennsylvania for Ireland is a credible informant-knowledge error — but that reasoning is completely absent from pe_005. Without it, the rules would cap the link at **`speculative`**, not `confident`.

#### Issue 3 — Rationale missing required structural elements
Two mandatory check lines are absent:
- **Date check:** No comparison between the certificate's implied birth year (~1845) and the tree person's attested birth year.
- **Residence check:** No confirmation that Schuylkill County, 1908, falls within the established geographic cluster.

---

### Recommended corrections (pending your authorization)
1. Add the date-check and residence-check lines.
2. Address the birthplace conflict explicitly in the rationale — cite the informant's secondary status and lack of birth knowledge as the reason it doesn't impair identity; clear `core_identifier_conflict` to null.
3. **Lower confidence from `confident` to `probable`.** The prior-record consistency (1850 and 1860 censuses of the same Patrick Flynn in Schuylkill County) qualitatively supports a solid `probable`. If `same_person` returns ≥ 0.75, `confident` could be re-earned.
4. Obtain and disclose the `match_score`.

---

### Also flagged (completeness gap)
`a_013` is a two-sided relationship (deceased ↔ father Thomas Flynn). Only the I1-side pe_ entry exists. There is no pe_ entry linking a_013 to Thomas Flynn — a separate linking task would be needed to close that gap.

---

**Bottom line:** The death certificate almost certainly does refer to your Patrick Flynn, but the link was written at a tier the current evidence doesn't support, and a conflicting birthplace was silently overlooked rather than cleared. Lowering to `probable` and adding the clearing explanation would make it both accurate and defensible. Would you like the agent to apply those corrections?

---

## Review of pe_005 (a_013 → I1, Patrick Flynn)

### What pe_005 actually links

a_013 is a `relationship` fact — "Father: Thomas Flynn" — extracted from the 1908 Pennsylvania death certificate (src_004 / ark:/61903/1:1:MDEF). The informant is James Brown, son-in-law, whose proximity is `family_not_present` and whose information quality is `secondary`. The rationale on pe_005 describes the whole death certificate as though a_013 were the death-event assertion itself; it is not. a_011 carries the death event (primary informant: attending physician); a_012 carries the birth information; a_013 carries the parentage relationship. The rationale conflates these.

---

### Issue 1 — Confidence calibration: `confident` is not supported

The match threshold rule is explicit: when identity rests on qualitative reasoning alone — without a `same_person` score of 0.75 or above — a single source supports **`probable` at most**, never `confident`. pe_005 has `match_score: null`, and the rationale gives no reason why the score was not obtained. If the persona "deceased" on this record was reachable (and all three assertions — a_011, a_012, a_013 — carry the same record persona), the writer now enforces that the score must have been obtained before the link was written. Either the call was skipped (a discipline failure) or the persona was not reachable (which the rationale must state). As it stands, `confident` is unjustified on the evidence on record. The appropriate ceiling is `probable`.

The other pe_ entries for I1 (pe_001 from the 1850 census, pe_004 from the 1860 census) also carry null scores, so the corroboration across those records is real but not formally quantified — it still supports that Patrick Flynn of Schuylkill County is I1, which makes the identity link on this death certificate stronger qualitatively. That prior-record consistency could firm up a `probable` link, but it cannot substitute for the missing score or elevate a single-source qualitative chain to `confident` on its own.

---

### Issue 2 — Unaddressed core identifier conflict

a_012 (birth information, same record, same deceased persona) carries an extraction note: "death cert says Pennsylvania, but census records say Ireland." A stated birthplace of Pennsylvania against prior census attestation of Ireland is a core identifier conflict. Under the threshold rules, that conflict must appear in the `core_identifier_conflict` field of every pe_ entry for this persona's assertions, unless the rationale explicitly clears it by explaining why the conflict does not impair the identity.

The extraction already provides a credible explanation: the informant (son-in-law, secondary, not present at the birth) plausibly did not know Patrick was born in Ireland and substituted Pennsylvania. That explanation, if accepted, would let the conflict be cleared — but pe_005's rationale says nothing about the birthplace discrepancy at all. The conflict is simply absent from the entry. Without that explicit clearing, pe_005 carries an unacknowledged conflict that, under the rules, would cap the link at `speculative`.

---

### Issue 3 — Rationale is missing required structural elements

Two check lines are required in every pe_ rationale before the tier is chosen:

- **Date check:** The death certificate gives a birth year of approximately 1845. What is the tree person's attested birth year, and what is the gap? This line is absent.
- **Residence check:** The record place is Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, 1908. What is the nearest attested prior residence on the tree person, and is this inside the cluster, neighbouring, or outside it with a measured distance? This line is absent.

Without these, a reviewer cannot verify that the place and date were actually compared before the tier was chosen.

---

### Issue 4 — Missing other-side pe_ link (completeness gap, not a calibration matter)

output.text_response:
The person-evidence agent was unable to copy the census facts onto I1 George Ackerman at this time. Here is its full report:

---

Both **pe_001** and **pe_002** now sit at `speculative`. With no link at `probable` or better from this record to any family member of I1 already in the tree, `materialize_facts` cannot write the census facts onto I1.

**What is blocking the write and what lifts it:**

A namesake cap exists because a second George Ackerman, born ~1825, is also recorded in Berks County (ns_001). The age of 42 in this census (~1818 birth) points to I1, not the namesake, but the cap requires the record to be tied to I1's family — meaning at least one other assertion from this same record must link at `probable` or better to I2 Catherine Ackerman (I1's wife) or to a known child of I1 already in the tree.

**The cap lifts in one of two ways:**

1. **Catherine appears in this census.** The 1860 census as currently extracted has only three roles: head_of_household (George), child_1 (Henry), and child_2 (Margaret). Catherine is absent from the extracted assertions. If she was enumerated in this household and her entry was simply not extracted, re-extracting the census record with a wife/spouse role and then linking that assertion to I2 at `probable` would immediately lift the cap and allow `materialize_facts` for George.

2. **Another record independently links I2 or a proven child to I1's family.** A second source — a marriage record for George and Catherine, or an earlier or later census including Catherine — that links to I2 at `probable` satisfies the tie and allows this census record's facts to reach I1.

**Catherine's absence** from this 1860 household is itself a question that needs answering: she may have died before 1860, been enumerated elsewhere, been separated, or this household may belong to the namesake rather than I1. That question should be opened before treating the census as confirmed for I1.

---

**Next step:** Determine why Catherine (I2) is absent from the 1860 Cumru Township census — whether she had already died, was listed elsewhere, or was simply not extracted from this record — so the household can be confirmed as belonging to George and Catherine, and the census facts can be properly applied to George in the tree.
